etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English sippen, of uncertain origin. Compare with Low German sippen (“to sip”). Possibly from a variant of Middle English suppen (“to drink, sip”) (see sup) or perhaps from Old English sipian, sypian (“to take in moisture, soak, macerate”), from Proto-Germanic *sipōną (“to drip, trickle”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, trickle, leak out”). Compare also Old High German supfen (“to drink, sip”), from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną (“to sip, intake”).

definitions.definition: An event at which people drink alcohol in small, usually sub-intoxicating amounts.

quote.citation: 1985 April 20, Joseph Beam, “Black Men Loving Black Men: The Revolutionary Act of the Eighties”, in Gay Community News, page 5:
quote.text: Earl is always a good time. His appearance at parties, whether it's a smart cocktail sip or a basement gig, is mandatory.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To drink slowly, small mouthfuls at a time.

quote.citation: [1898], J[ohn] Meade Falkner, “In the Vault”, in Moonfleet, London; Toronto, Ont.: Jonathan Cape, published 1934, →OCLC, pages 62–63:
quote.text: He held out to me a bowl of steaming broth, that filled the room with a savour sweeter, ten thousand times, to me than every rose and lily of the world; yet would not let me drink it at a gulp, but made me sip it with a spoon like any baby.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 5, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: A waiter brought his aperitif, which was a small scotch and soda, and as he sipped it gratefully he sighed.

quote.citation: 2013 August 3, “Revenge of the nerds”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8847:
quote.text: bright young things in jeans and T-shirts huddle around laptops, sipping lattes or munching on free food.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Second Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: [She] rais'd it to her mouth with sober grace; / Then, sipping, offered to the next in place.

definitions.definition: To taste the liquor of; to drink out of.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Fourth Book of the Georgics”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: They skim the floods, and sip the purple flowers.

definitions.definition: (Scotland, US, dated) Alternative form of seep

quote.citation: 1995, Richard North, Life on a Modern Planet: A Manifesto for Progress‎[1], Manchester University Press, →ISBN, page 80:
quote.text: Sales of lightbulbs which sip electricity, and whose increased cost in the shops is easily paid for over their lifetime, used to double every year; in 1990/1991, they leapt sevenfold.

quote.citation: 2008 July 3, “The presidential election: White men can vote”, in The Economist‎[2]:
quote.text: It makes a small car, the Chevy Cobalt, which sips petrol in moderation and is therefore selling well.

quote.citation: 2014 October 20, Erik Hyrkas, "Energy Vampires are Attacking Your Home – Here’s How to Stop Them" (Office of Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy)
quote.text: Even when turned off, these devices can idly sip electricity from your outlet costing you money.
